## Visualizing the Four Main Data Types in Statistics
   This R code generates synthetic datasets representing
   the four types of data used in statistics:
     1) Continuous (Quantitative)
     2) Discrete (Quantitative)
     3) Nominal (Qualitative)
     4) Ordinal (Qualitative)

   Each dataset is visualized using appropriate plots:
     - Histogram (Continuous)
     - Bar Plot (Discrete)
     - Bar Plot (Nominal)
     - Ordered Bar Plot (Ordinal)

   This code is compatible with RMarkdown (.Rmd) and
   produces clean, educational graphics using ggplot2.

```{r, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Load required libraries
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(forcats)
library(gridExtra)

set.seed(123)

# -------------------------------
# 1. Continuous Data (e.g., Height)
# -------------------------------
height <- rnorm(500, mean = 170, sd = 10)  # Normally distributed heights
continuous_df <- data.frame(Height = height)

p1 <- ggplot(continuous_df, aes(x = Height)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "black", fill = "#4682B4", bins = 25) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(Height)), color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Continuous Data: Height Distribution",
    subtitle = "Normally distributed (mean = 170, sd = 10)",
    x = "Height (cm)", y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

# -------------------------------
# 2. Discrete Data (e.g., Number of Defects)
# -------------------------------
defects <- rpois(300, lambda = 3)  # Poisson distribution
discrete_df <- data.frame(Defects = defects)

p2 <- ggplot(discrete_df, aes(x = as.factor(Defects))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#FF8C00", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Discrete Data: Number of Defects per Batch",
    subtitle = "Poisson-distributed (λ = 3)",
    x = "Number of Defects", y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

# -------------------------------
# 3. Nominal Data (e.g., Favorite Color)
# -------------------------------
colors <- c("Red", "Blue", "Green", "Yellow", "Purple")
favorite_color <- sample(colors, 400, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.25, 0.30, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10))
nominal_df <- data.frame(Color = favorite_color)

p3 <- ggplot(nominal_df, aes(x = Color, fill = Color)) +
  geom_bar(color = "black") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title = "Nominal Data: Favorite Color",
    subtitle = "Categorical data with no inherent order",
    x = "Color", y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# -------------------------------
# 4. Ordinal Data (e.g., Satisfaction Level)
# -------------------------------
levels_order <- c("Very Unsatisfied", "Unsatisfied", "Neutral", "Satisfied", "Very Satisfied")
satisfaction <- sample(levels_order, 400, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.40, 0.25))
ordinal_df <- data.frame(Satisfaction = factor(satisfaction, levels = levels_order))

p4 <- ggplot(ordinal_df, aes(x = Satisfaction, fill = Satisfaction)) +
  geom_bar(color = "black") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdYlGn") +
  labs(
    title = "Ordinal Data: Customer Satisfaction",
    subtitle = "Ordered categories (Low → High)",
    x = "Satisfaction Level", y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1), legend.position = "none")

# -------------------------------
# Combine all plots
# -------------------------------
grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, p4, ncol = 2)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# End of Script
# -----------------------------------------------------------
```
